title: Respiration & Photosynthesis
description: Enzymes and inhibitors, glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, the ETC and chemiosmosis, ATP yield, fermentation, light reactions, the Calvin cycle, C4 and CAM.

cards.title: Enzymes speed up chemical reactions by lowering what?
cards.body:
The activation energy ($E_A$), the energy needed to reach the transition state.

Enzymes don't change $\Delta G$, so they can't make an endergonic reaction spontaneous. They only speed up reactions that would happen anyway.

Key idea: enzymes aren't used up in the reaction, and each is **specific** to its substrates.
cards.searchQuery: enzymes lower activation energy transition state catalysis

cards.title: An enzyme inhibitor's effect can be overcome by adding more substrate. What type of inhibitor is it?
cards.body:
A competitive inhibitor.

It resembles the substrate and **competes for the active site**, so enough extra substrate outcompetes it.

Watch out: a **noncompetitive** inhibitor binds elsewhere and changes the enzyme's shape, making the active site less effective. Extra substrate doesn't help.
cards.searchQuery: competitive inhibition vs noncompetitive enzyme inhibitor active site

cards.title: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
cards.body:
2 ATP.

Glycolysis makes 4 ATP by **substrate-level phosphorylation** and invests 2 ATP early on, so the net gain is 2. It also yields 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate.

Key idea: it runs in the cytosol and doesn't need $\ce{O2}$.
cards.searchQuery: glycolysis net ATP yield per glucose 2 ATP 2 NADH

cards.title: Pyruvate oxidation converts each pyruvate into what molecule, which then enters the citric acid cycle?
cards.body:
Acetyl CoA.

In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate loses a carbon as $\ce{CO2}$, the remaining two-carbon fragment is oxidized (with $\ce{NAD+}$ reduced to $\ce{NADH}$), and coenzyme A is attached.

Example: per glucose this makes 2 acetyl CoA, 2 $\ce{CO2}$ and 2 NADH.
cards.searchQuery: pyruvate oxidation acetyl CoA mitochondrial matrix

cards.title: Per glucose (two turns), what does the citric acid cycle produce?
cards.body:
2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 $\ce{FADH2}$ and 4 $\ce{CO2}$.

Per turn: 1 ATP, 3 NADH, 1 $\ce{FADH2}$ and 2 $\ce{CO2}$. It runs in the mitochondrial matrix.

Watch out: with pyruvate oxidation's 2 $\ce{CO2}$, all six carbons of glucose leave as $\ce{CO2}$. In some cells the cycle's one substrate-level phosphorylation step makes GTP instead of ATP.
cards.searchQuery: citric acid cycle yield per glucose NADH FADH2 ATP CO2

cards.title: What is the final electron acceptor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain?
cards.body:
$\ce{O2}$

It picks up electrons and $\ce{H+}$ to form water. The chain is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae).

Why: without $\ce{O2}$ the chain stalls, NADH can't be reoxidized, and cells must rely on fermentation. Cyanide kills by blocking electron transfer to $\ce{O2}$.
cards.searchQuery: final electron acceptor electron transport chain oxygen water

cards.title: In mitochondria, the electron transport chain pumps $\ce{H+}$ out of the matrix into which compartment?
cards.body:
The intermembrane space.

$\ce{H+}$ flows back down its gradient into the matrix through **ATP synthase**, which uses this proton-motive force to make ATP from ADP and phosphate. This is chemiosmosis.

Key idea: together with the ETC it forms oxidative phosphorylation, which makes almost $90\%$ of respiration's ATP.
cards.searchQuery: mitochondria intermembrane space proton gradient chemiosmosis ATP synthase

cards.title: About how many ATP does aerobic respiration yield per glucose, and why isn't it an exact whole number?
cards.body:
About $30$–$32$ ATP in current textbooks (older ones say $36$–$38$).

Each NADH gives about $2.5$ ATP and each $\ce{FADH2}$ about $1.5$. NADH made in glycolysis yields less if a shuttle passes its electrons to FAD.

Watch out: some of the proton-motive force powers other work, so the number is an estimate. This captures roughly a third of glucose's chemical energy.
cards.searchQuery: ATP yield per glucose aerobic respiration 30 to 32 not exact

cards.title: Fermentation makes no ATP beyond glycolysis. So what does it accomplish for a cell without $\ce{O2}$?
cards.body:
It regenerates $\ce{NAD+}$ from NADH, so glycolysis can keep running (net 2 ATP per glucose).

Lactic acid fermentation: pyruvate is reduced to lactate (muscle cells, some bacteria). Alcohol fermentation: pyruvate loses $\ce{CO2}$ to form acetaldehyde, which is reduced to ethanol (yeast).

Key idea: no $\ce{NAD+}$ means no glycolysis, so recycling it is the whole point.
cards.searchQuery: fermentation regenerates NAD+ glycolysis lactic acid alcohol

cards.title: The $\ce{O2}$ released by photosynthesis comes from splitting which molecule?
cards.body:
Water ($\ce{H2O}$).

Photosystem II splits water to replace the electrons lost by its P680 reaction center. The $\ce{H+}$ goes into the thylakoid space and $\ce{O2}$ is released.

Why: $\ce{^{18}O}$ tracer experiments confirmed it. Labeled water gives labeled $\ce{O2}$, but labeled $\ce{CO2}$ doesn't, because $\ce{CO2}$'s oxygen ends up in sugar and new water.
cards.searchQuery: photosynthesis oxygen comes from water splitting photosystem II

cards.title: In linear electron flow, which photosystem is the first to absorb light and pass electrons down the chain?
cards.body:
Photosystem II (reaction center P680).

Its electrons pass through an electron transport chain (plastoquinone, a cytochrome complex, plastocyanin) to **photosystem I** (P700), then to $\ce{NADP+}$, forming NADPH. The $\ce{H+}$ gradient built along the way drives ATP synthesis.

Watch out: the photosystems are numbered in order of discovery, not order of action. All of this happens in the thylakoid membranes.
cards.searchQuery: linear electron flow photosystem II first P680 photosystem I P700

cards.title: In which part of the chloroplast does the Calvin cycle take place?
cards.body:
The stroma, the fluid surrounding the thylakoids.

The Calvin cycle spends the ATP and NADPH made by the light reactions in the thylakoid membranes.

Tip: thylakoid means light reactions, stroma means Calvin cycle (just as the mitochondrial matrix holds the citric acid cycle).
cards.searchQuery: Calvin cycle location chloroplast stroma thylakoid

cards.title: Which enzyme catalyzes carbon fixation, the first step of the Calvin cycle, and is probably the most abundant protein on Earth?
cards.body:
Rubisco (RuBP carboxylase-oxygenase).

It attaches $\ce{CO2}$ to the 5-carbon sugar RuBP. The unstable 6-carbon product immediately splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate.

Watch out: rubisco can also bind $\ce{O2}$ instead of $\ce{CO2}$, which causes photorespiration.
cards.searchQuery: rubisco carbon fixation Calvin cycle most abundant protein

cards.title: To make one net G3P from $3$ $\ce{CO2}$, how many ATP and NADPH does the Calvin cycle use?
cards.body:
$9$ ATP and $6$ NADPH.

Phases: carbon fixation (rubisco), reduction ($6$ ATP and $6$ NADPH turn 3-phosphoglycerate into G3P), and regeneration of RuBP ($3$ ATP).

Example: the equivalent of one glucose takes 2 G3P, which means $6$ $\ce{CO2}$, $18$ ATP and $12$ NADPH.
cards.searchQuery: Calvin cycle ATP NADPH cost per G3P 9 ATP 6 NADPH

cards.title: On hot, dry days a C3 plant closes its stomata, and rubisco starts adding $\ce{O2}$ instead of $\ce{CO2}$ to RuBP. What is this wasteful process?
cards.body:
Photorespiration.

It consumes $\ce{O2}$ and releases $\ce{CO2}$ but makes no ATP and no sugar. It can drain as much as $50\%$ of the carbon fixed by the Calvin cycle.

Watch out: C3 crops such as rice, wheat and soybeans are vulnerable. C4 and CAM plants minimize it.
cards.searchQuery: photorespiration rubisco oxygen C3 plants hot dry wasteful

cards.title: How do C4 plants and CAM plants each keep initial $\ce{CO2}$ fixation separate from the Calvin cycle?
cards.body:
C4 separates them in **space**, CAM in **time**.

C4 (corn, sugarcane): PEP carboxylase fixes $\ce{CO2}$ into 4-carbon compounds in mesophyll cells, which pass them to bundle-sheath cells that release $\ce{CO2}$ to the Calvin cycle.

CAM (cacti, pineapple): stomata open at night and $\ce{CO2}$ is stored as organic acids. By day, with stomata closed, the same cells release it to the Calvin cycle.
cards.searchQuery: C4 vs CAM photosynthesis space vs time CO2 fixation

cards.title: What term describes the sum of all the chemical reactions in an organism?
cards.body:
Metabolism.

It includes pathways that **break down** molecules to release energy and pathways that **build** molecules using energy. Each step is catalyzed by a specific enzyme.

Key idea: metabolism manages the cell's materials and energy.
cards.searchQuery: metabolism definition sum of all chemical reactions in organism

cards.title: What do we call metabolic pathways that break down complex molecules into simpler ones and release energy?
cards.body:
Catabolic pathways.

Cellular respiration is the standard example: glucose is broken down and some of its energy is captured in ATP.

Mnemonic: **cata**bolic = **cut** down; **ana**bolic = **add** up.
cards.searchQuery: catabolic pathways break down molecules release energy cellular respiration

cards.title: What do we call metabolic pathways that build complex molecules from simpler ones, using energy?
cards.body:
Anabolic pathways.

They consume energy to **build** products such as proteins from amino acids and sugars from $\ce{CO2}$ in photosynthesis.

Key idea: energy released by catabolic pathways drives anabolic pathways.
cards.searchQuery: anabolic pathways build complex molecules consume energy examples

cards.title: What term describes a reaction that releases free energy, with $\Delta G < 0$?
cards.body:
Exergonic.

The products have **less free energy** than the reactants, and the reaction can proceed spontaneously, though not necessarily quickly.

Example: cellular respiration, with $\Delta G \approx -686\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$ per mole of glucose.
cards.searchQuery: exergonic reaction negative delta G releases free energy

cards.title: What term describes a reaction that absorbs free energy from its surroundings, with $\Delta G > 0$?
cards.body:
Endergonic.

The products have **more free energy** than the reactants, so the reaction is nonspontaneous unless energy is supplied.

Example: photosynthesis stores about $686\,\mathrm{kcal}$ per mole of glucose made, using light energy.
cards.searchQuery: endergonic reaction positive delta G absorbs free energy

cards.title: What three components make up an ATP molecule?
cards.body:
Adenine, ribose, and a chain of three phosphate groups.

Adenine plus ribose makes the nucleoside **adenosine**. The phosphate groups are all negatively charged, so they repel each other and the chain is unstable.

Key idea: removing the terminal phosphate releases energy to do cellular work.
cards.searchQuery: ATP structure adenine ribose three phosphate groups

cards.title: How does the cell use ATP hydrolysis to drive an endergonic reaction?
cards.body:
ATP transfers its terminal phosphate group to a reactant, in a step called phosphorylation.

The **phosphorylated intermediate** has more free energy and can then react. The overall coupled process is exergonic.

Example: under standard conditions, hydrolyzing ATP to ADP and $\mathrm{P_i}$ has $\Delta G \approx -7.3\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$ ($-30.5\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$), and in cells it is even more negative.
cards.searchQuery: ATP energy coupling phosphorylation hydrolysis drives endergonic reactions

cards.title: Which law of thermodynamics states that energy can be transferred and transformed but not created or destroyed?
cards.body:
The first law (conservation of energy).

In a cell, energy changes form: light becomes chemical energy in photosynthesis, and chemical energy becomes ATP, work and **heat** in respiration.

Key idea: the total energy of the universe stays constant.
cards.searchQuery: first law of thermodynamics conservation of energy biology

cards.title: What does the second law of thermodynamics say about every energy transfer or transformation?
cards.body:
It increases the entropy (disorder) of the universe.

Some energy is always lost as **heat**, so no conversion is $100\%$ efficient. This is why cells need a continuous supply of energy.

Watch out: a cell can become more ordered, but only by increasing disorder in its surroundings, mostly by releasing heat.
cards.searchQuery: second law of thermodynamics entropy heat loss living cells

cards.title: Write the equation relating the change in free energy to enthalpy, temperature and entropy.
cards.body:
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\,\Delta S$

Here $\Delta G$ is the change in free energy, $\Delta H$ the change in enthalpy (total energy), $T$ the absolute temperature in kelvins, and $\Delta S$ the change in entropy.

Key idea: a process is spontaneous when $\Delta G < 0$. A more negative $\Delta H$ and a more positive $\Delta S$ both help.
cards.searchQuery: Gibbs free energy equation delta G equals delta H minus T delta S

cards.title: What is the region of an enzyme where the substrate binds and the reaction takes place?
cards.body:
The active site.

It is usually a pocket formed by a few amino acids, and its shape and chemistry make the enzyme **specific** to its substrate.

Watch out: the active site is different from an allosteric site, which regulates the enzyme from somewhere else.
cards.searchQuery: enzyme active site substrate binding pocket specificity

cards.title: When a substrate binds, the enzyme's active site changes shape slightly to grip it more tightly. What is this model called?
cards.body:
Induced fit.

The tighter fit brings chemical groups into position to **catalyze** the reaction, for instance by straining bonds in the substrate.

Key idea: this refines the older lock-and-key picture, in which the active site was thought to be rigid.
cards.searchQuery: induced fit model enzyme substrate active site change shape

cards.title: How does temperature affect an enzyme's reaction rate, and what happens above the optimum?
cards.body:
The rate rises with temperature up to an optimum, then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures.

Warmer temperatures increase molecular collisions, but past the optimum, **agitation breaks the bonds** that hold the enzyme's 3D shape.

Example: human enzymes work best near $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, while enzymes of hot-spring bacteria have much higher optima.
cards.searchQuery: enzyme activity temperature optimum denaturation rate graph

cards.title: Why do different enzymes have different optimal pH values, such as pepsin near pH $2$ and trypsin near pH $8$?
cards.body:
Each enzyme's shape and active-site charges work best in the environment where it normally operates.

pH alters the **ionization of amino acid side chains**, which can distort the enzyme's shape. Pepsin works in the acidic stomach and trypsin in the small intestine.

Key idea: extreme pH values denature most enzymes.
cards.searchQuery: enzyme optimum pH pepsin trypsin stomach small intestine

cards.title: What is the loss of a protein's native three-dimensional shape, and with it its function, called?
cards.body:
Denaturation.

Heat, extreme pH or certain chemicals disrupt the **weak bonds** that maintain the 3D structure, so the active site no longer fits the substrate.

Watch out: denaturation changes the shape but doesn't break the peptide bonds of the primary structure.
cards.searchQuery: protein denaturation enzyme loses shape heat pH function

cards.title: What are organic, nonprotein helpers of enzymes, such as many vitamin-derived molecules, called?
cards.body:
Coenzymes.

They bind to the enzyme (often at the active site) and carry **electrons or small groups** between reactions. Inorganic helpers such as $\ce{Zn^2+}$ or $\ce{Mg^2+}$ are cofactors that aren't coenzymes.

Example: $\ce{NAD+}$ is derived from the vitamin niacin.
cards.searchQuery: coenzyme definition vitamins cofactor NAD+ enzyme helpers

cards.title: What is it called when a regulatory molecule binds at a site other than the active site and changes an enzyme's activity?
cards.body:
Allosteric regulation.

Binding of an **activator** stabilizes the active shape, while an **inhibitor** stabilizes the inactive shape.

Example: ATP and ADP often act as allosteric regulators of respiration enzymes, linking the pathway's rate to the cell's energy needs.
cards.searchQuery: allosteric regulation enzyme activator inhibitor regulatory site

cards.title: When the end product of a metabolic pathway inhibits an enzyme early in that pathway, what is this regulation called?
cards.body:
Feedback inhibition.

When the product builds up, it shuts down its own production, which **prevents waste** of resources. When it is used up, the pathway turns back on.

Example: ATP inhibits an early enzyme of glycolysis, slowing the pathway when the cell has plenty of ATP.
cards.searchQuery: feedback inhibition end product metabolic pathway enzyme regulation

cards.title: Why does an enzyme's reaction rate level off at high substrate concentration?
cards.body:
All of the enzyme's active sites are occupied.

The enzyme is **saturated**: it works at its maximum rate, so adding more substrate doesn't speed things up.

Tip: the rate then rises only with more enzyme.
cards.searchQuery: enzyme saturation substrate concentration maximum rate active sites

cards.title: Write the overall equation for aerobic cellular respiration of glucose.
cards.body:
$\ce{C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O}$ + energy (ATP and heat)

The reaction is exergonic, with $\Delta G \approx -686\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$ of glucose. About a third of that energy is captured in ATP and the rest is released as heat.

Watch out: it is the reverse of the photosynthesis equation, but it is **not** the reverse reaction pathway. The two use different steps.
cards.searchQuery: cellular respiration overall equation glucose oxygen carbon dioxide water ATP

cards.title: In a redox reaction, a substance that loses electrons is said to be what?
cards.body:
Oxidized.

**Oxidation** is loss of electrons, and **reduction** is gain of electrons. The two always occur together.

Mnemonic: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.
cards.searchQuery: oxidation loss of electrons redox OIL RIG

cards.title: In a redox reaction, a substance that gains electrons is said to be what?
cards.body:
Reduced.

Gaining electrons lowers the atom's charge, hence the term "reduction". In respiration, $\ce{NAD+}$ is reduced to $\ce{NADH}$.

Watch out: the electron donor is the **reducing agent**, and it is the one that gets oxidized.
cards.searchQuery: reduction gain of electrons redox reducing agent NAD+ NADH

cards.title: In cellular respiration, which molecule is oxidized and which is reduced?
cards.body:
Glucose is oxidized and $\ce{O2}$ is reduced.

Glucose loses electrons (with their hydrogens) and becomes $\ce{CO2}$, while $\ce{O2}$ gains them and becomes $\ce{H2O}$.

Why: electrons in C–H bonds are at high energy, and moving toward oxygen, which is very electronegative, releases that energy for ATP synthesis.
cards.searchQuery: cellular respiration redox glucose oxidized oxygen reduced

cards.title: What role does $\ce{NAD+}$ play in cellular respiration?
cards.body:
It is an electron carrier (oxidizing agent) that is reduced to $\ce{NADH}$.

$\ce{NAD+}$ accepts a pair of electrons and a proton from a substrate, then **delivers the electrons** to the electron transport chain.

Key idea: NADH is like a rechargeable battery, carrying high-energy electrons to where they can make ATP.
cards.searchQuery: NAD+ NADH electron carrier cellular respiration role

cards.title: Name the four stages of aerobic respiration in order.
cards.body:
Glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.

Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol. The other three occur in the **mitochondria**: pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle in the matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation at the inner membrane.

Tip: count the carbons. $6$ in glucose, $3$ in pyruvate, $2$ in acetyl CoA, and $0$ left after the cycle.
cards.searchQuery: stages of cellular respiration glycolysis citric acid cycle oxidative phosphorylation

cards.title: What is the direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate molecule to ADP by an enzyme called?
cards.body:
Substrate-level phosphorylation.

It makes ATP without a proton gradient. It occurs in **glycolysis** and once per turn of the citric acid cycle.

Watch out: it accounts for only a small fraction of respiration's ATP, so don't confuse it with oxidative phosphorylation.
cards.searchQuery: substrate-level phosphorylation definition glycolysis citric acid cycle ATP

cards.title: What is the process in which the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis together produce ATP?
cards.body:
Oxidative phosphorylation.

Energy released by electrons moving down the ETC builds an $\ce{H+}$ gradient, and **ATP synthase** uses the gradient to phosphorylate ADP.

Key idea: it makes about $26$–$28$ of the $30$–$32$ ATP per glucose.
cards.searchQuery: oxidative phosphorylation electron transport chain chemiosmosis ATP synthesis

cards.title: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?
cards.body:
The cytosol.

Glycolysis needs no organelle, which fits its ancient origin. It is found in **nearly all cells**, from bacteria to humans.

Watch out: pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle are the steps that occur in the mitochondrion.
cards.searchQuery: glycolysis location cytosol cell anaerobic pathway

cards.title: Glycolysis splits the 6-carbon glucose into two molecules of which 3-carbon compound?
cards.body:
Pyruvate.

Glycolysis ("splitting of sugar") has an energy investment phase and an energy **payoff phase**, producing 2 pyruvate, 2 ATP (net) and 2 NADH.

Key idea: pyruvate is also the crossroads. With $\ce{O2}$ it goes to the mitochondria; without it, to fermentation.
cards.searchQuery: glycolysis glucose to pyruvate 3-carbon products

cards.title: What features of glycolysis suggest it is an evolutionarily ancient pathway?
cards.body:
It occurs in the cytosol without organelles and doesn't require $\ce{O2}$.

Early life arose when the atmosphere had little $\ce{O2}$, and glycolysis is present in **nearly all organisms**, including prokaryotes.

Key idea: the machinery for aerobic respiration evolved later, after $\ce{O2}$ accumulated.
cards.searchQuery: glycolysis ancient pathway evolution no oxygen no organelles

cards.title: How does aerobic respiration differ from anaerobic respiration?
cards.body:
Aerobic respiration uses $\ce{O2}$ as the final electron acceptor. Anaerobic respiration uses a different inorganic molecule.

Both use an **electron transport chain**. Some prokaryotes use sulfate ($\ce{SO4^2-}$) as the acceptor.

Watch out: anaerobic respiration is not the same as fermentation, which has no electron transport chain.
cards.searchQuery: aerobic vs anaerobic respiration final electron acceptor sulfate fermentation

cards.title: In which compartment of a eukaryotic cell does the citric acid cycle take place?
cards.body:
The mitochondrial matrix.

The cycle's enzymes are in the matrix (one is in the inner membrane), the same compartment where **pyruvate oxidation** occurs.

Watch out: in prokaryotes there are no mitochondria, so the cycle takes place in the cytosol.
cards.searchQuery: citric acid cycle location mitochondrial matrix

cards.title: In the first step of the citric acid cycle, acetyl CoA combines with which 4-carbon compound to form citrate?
cards.body:
Oxaloacetate.

Acetyl CoA adds its 2-carbon acetyl group to oxaloacetate to make 6-carbon **citrate**. The last step of the cycle regenerates oxaloacetate.

Key idea: that regeneration is why it is called a cycle.
cards.searchQuery: citric acid cycle acetyl CoA oxaloacetate citrate first step

cards.title: Counting pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle, how many molecules of $\ce{CO2}$ are released per glucose?
cards.body:
$6$

Pyruvate oxidation releases 2 $\ce{CO2}$ (one per pyruvate) and the cycle releases 4 (two per turn, two turns).

Key idea: all six carbons of glucose end up as $\ce{CO2}$. That's the carbon you exhale.
cards.searchQuery: CO2 released per glucose pyruvate oxidation citric acid cycle six carbons

cards.title: Counting glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation and the citric acid cycle, how many NADH and $\ce{FADH2}$ are made per glucose?
cards.body:
$10$ NADH and $2$ $\ce{FADH2}$.

NADH: $2$ from glycolysis, $2$ from pyruvate oxidation and $6$ from the citric acid cycle. $\ce{FADH2}$: all $2$ from the cycle.

Tip: these carriers deliver the electrons to the electron transport chain, where most ATP is made.
cards.searchQuery: NADH FADH2 total per glucose glycolysis pyruvate oxidation citric acid cycle

cards.title: How can the cell get energy from fats and proteins through the pathways of respiration?
cards.body:
Fats and proteins are broken into units that enter respiration at different points.

Fatty acids are converted to **acetyl CoA** (beta oxidation), and amino acids lose their amino group and then enter as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or citric acid cycle intermediates.

Key idea: glycolysis and the citric acid cycle are a central hub of catabolism.
cards.searchQuery: catabolism of fats and proteins enter cellular respiration acetyl CoA

cards.title: Why does a gram of fat store more than twice the energy of a gram of carbohydrate?
cards.body:
Fat has many more energy-rich C–H bonds and is less oxidized.

Fatty acids hold more hydrogen per carbon, so their oxidation can pass **more electrons** to carriers. Fat has about $9\,\mathrm{kcal/g}$ and carbohydrate about $4\,\mathrm{kcal/g}$.

Tip: this is why fat is the body's long-term energy store.
cards.searchQuery: fat vs carbohydrate energy per gram more C-H bonds energy storage

cards.title: After its discoverer, what other name is the citric acid cycle known by?
cards.body:
The Krebs cycle.

Hans Krebs worked out the cycle in the 1930s. It is also called the **TCA cycle** (tricarboxylic acid cycle).

Key idea: all three names refer to the same pathway.
cards.searchQuery: Krebs cycle citric acid cycle TCA cycle same pathway Hans Krebs

cards.title: In eukaryotic cells, where is the electron transport chain located?
cards.body:
The inner mitochondrial membrane.

The membrane is folded into **cristae**, which increase the surface area so more electron transport chains and ATP synthases fit.

Watch out: in prokaryotes the chain is in the plasma membrane.
cards.searchQuery: electron transport chain location inner mitochondrial membrane cristae

cards.title: Which carriers deliver electrons to the electron transport chain, and which of them enters later?
cards.body:
$\ce{NADH}$ and $\ce{FADH2}$. $\ce{FADH2}$ enters later in the chain.

NADH passes its electrons to the first complex of the chain, while $\ce{FADH2}$ passes them to a **later** complex.

Key idea: the entry point determines how many protons are pumped per carrier.
cards.searchQuery: NADH FADH2 electron transport chain entry complex I complex II

cards.title: How does the electron transport chain use the energy released as electrons pass from carrier to carrier?
cards.body:
It pumps $\ce{H+}$ across the membrane, building a proton gradient.

Electrons move toward carriers that are more **electronegative**, losing energy in small steps. The chain doesn't make ATP directly.

Watch out: the large controlled steps avoid the explosive release that would happen if $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{O2}$ reacted in one step.
cards.searchQuery: electron transport chain energy release proton pumping gradient no direct ATP

cards.title: Which enzyme complex uses the flow of $\ce{H+}$ down its gradient to make ATP from ADP and $\mathrm{P_i}$?
cards.body:
ATP synthase.

It acts like a **molecular turbine**: $\ce{H+}$ passing through it makes part of the complex rotate, and that rotation drives the phosphorylation of ADP.

Key idea: the same enzyme works in mitochondria, chloroplasts and bacteria.
cards.searchQuery: ATP synthase enzyme proton gradient rotation makes ATP

cards.title: What name is given to the potential energy stored in an $\ce{H+}$ gradient across a membrane, which can drive ATP synthesis?
cards.body:
Proton-motive force.

It arises from both a **concentration difference** of $\ce{H+}$ and a charge difference across the membrane.

Key idea: a cell can use it to make ATP, but also to power other work.
cards.searchQuery: proton-motive force definition H+ gradient potential energy membrane

cards.title: What is the energy-coupling mechanism that uses the energy stored in an $\ce{H+}$ gradient across a membrane to drive cellular work called?
cards.body:
Chemiosmosis.

In mitochondria and chloroplasts, $\ce{H+}$ flows down its gradient through ATP synthase to make ATP.

Key idea: the term was introduced by Peter Mitchell, who proposed it in 1961.
cards.searchQuery: chemiosmosis definition Peter Mitchell proton gradient ATP synthesis

cards.title: Why does $\ce{FADH2}$ yield less ATP than NADH?
cards.body:
It donates its electrons at a later point in the chain, so fewer $\ce{H+}$ are pumped.

The electrons skip the first proton-pumping step, which means less proton-motive force is built per $\ce{FADH2}$.

Example: about $1.5$ ATP per $\ce{FADH2}$ versus about $2.5$ ATP per NADH.
cards.searchQuery: why FADH2 yields less ATP than NADH electron transport chain entry point

cards.title: In aerobic prokaryotes with no mitochondria, where is the electron transport chain and where are protons pumped?
cards.body:
The chain is in the plasma membrane and pumps $\ce{H+}$ out of the cell.

The gradient across the **plasma membrane** drives ATP synthase, just as the inner mitochondrial membrane does in eukaryotes.

Key idea: this supports the endosymbiont origin of mitochondria.
cards.searchQuery: prokaryote electron transport chain plasma membrane proton gradient

cards.title: What happens to the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain when $\ce{O2}$ is absent?
cards.body:
Both stop, because the ETC backs up.

With no $\ce{O2}$ to accept electrons, NADH can't be oxidized back to $\ce{NAD+}$, so the cycle (which needs $\ce{NAD+}$) slows.

Key idea: that's why a cell without $\ce{O2}$ must ferment to keep glycolysis going.
cards.searchQuery: no oxygen electron transport chain stops citric acid cycle NAD+ regeneration

cards.title: What happens if the inner mitochondrial membrane becomes leaky to $\ce{H+}$, as with brown fat's uncoupling protein?
cards.body:
The gradient collapses, so less ATP is made and the energy is released as heat.

Electron transport continues, but $\ce{H+}$ flows back **without passing through ATP synthase**.

Example: newborn mammals and hibernators use this in brown fat to generate body heat.
cards.searchQuery: uncoupling protein brown fat thermogenesis proton leak heat instead of ATP

cards.title: What is the end product of lactic acid fermentation, formed when pyruvate is reduced by NADH?
cards.body:
Lactate.

Pyruvate accepts electrons from NADH, which regenerates $\ce{NAD+}$. No $\ce{CO2}$ is released in this process.

Example: muscle cells do this in intense exercise. The lactate is later carried to the liver and converted back to pyruvate when $\ce{O2}$ is available.
cards.searchQuery: lactic acid fermentation lactate pyruvate NADH muscle cells

cards.title: Which gas released by yeast during alcohol fermentation makes bread dough rise?
cards.body:
$\ce{CO2}$

Yeast removes a carbon from pyruvate as $\ce{CO2}$, leaving acetaldehyde, which NADH reduces to **ethanol**. The $\ce{CO2}$ bubbles make dough rise and beer fizzy.

Key idea: the ethanol evaporates during baking.
cards.searchQuery: alcohol fermentation yeast carbon dioxide bread dough rise ethanol

cards.title: What do we call an organism that can make ATP by fermentation or by aerobic respiration, depending on whether $\ce{O2}$ is present?
cards.body:
A facultative anaerobe.

It uses $\ce{O2}$ when available (more ATP) and switches to fermentation when it isn't.

Example: yeast and many bacteria, and our own muscle cells behave in this way.
cards.searchQuery: facultative anaerobe definition fermentation or aerobic respiration yeast

cards.title: What name is given to organisms that carry out only fermentation or anaerobic respiration and are poisoned by $\ce{O2}$?
cards.body:
Obligate anaerobes.

They can't use $\ce{O2}$ and cannot survive in its presence.

Example: the bacterium that causes botulism and bacteria in deep mud.
cards.searchQuery: obligate anaerobe definition poisoned by oxygen fermentation

cards.title: Roughly how does the ATP yield of aerobic respiration compare with that of fermentation, per glucose?
cards.body:
Respiration yields roughly $15$ times more: about $30$ ATP versus $2$.

Fermentation only uses glycolysis, and the glucose is only **partly oxidized**. Much of the energy remains in lactate or ethanol.

Why: that's why fermenting cells must consume glucose at a much higher rate.
cards.searchQuery: ATP yield fermentation vs aerobic respiration comparison per glucose

cards.title: In fermentation, what serves as the final electron acceptor for NADH?
cards.body:
An organic molecule, pyruvate or a derivative of it.

Pyruvate itself accepts the electrons in lactic acid fermentation, and **acetaldehyde** (made from pyruvate) does in alcohol fermentation.

Watch out: no electron transport chain is involved, so no ATP is made from NADH.
cards.searchQuery: fermentation final electron acceptor pyruvate acetaldehyde organic molecule

cards.title: Write the overall equation for photosynthesis.
cards.body:
$\ce{6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2}$ (powered by light)

Light energy is stored in sugar: the reaction is endergonic, with $\Delta G \approx +686\,\mathrm{kcal/mol}$ of glucose.

Key idea: it is the opposite of respiration's equation. Water is oxidized and $\ce{CO2}$ is reduced.
cards.searchQuery: photosynthesis overall equation carbon dioxide water glucose oxygen light

cards.title: What term describes organisms that make their own organic molecules from $\ce{CO2}$ and other inorganic raw materials?
cards.body:
Autotrophs.

They are the **producers** of an ecosystem. Photoautotrophs such as plants, algae and cyanobacteria use light energy.

Watch out: some autotrophs, called chemoautotrophs, use energy from inorganic chemicals instead of light.
cards.searchQuery: autotrophs definition producers photoautotrophs make organic molecules from CO2

cards.title: What term describes organisms that obtain organic molecules by consuming other organisms or their products?
cards.body:
Heterotrophs.

They are the **consumers** and decomposers of an ecosystem, and animals and fungi are examples.

Key idea: nearly all heterotrophs depend on autotrophs for the organic molecules and $\ce{O2}$ they use.
cards.searchQuery: heterotrophs definition consumers obtain organic molecules from other organisms

cards.title: What are the stacks of thylakoids inside a chloroplast called?
cards.body:
Grana (singular, granum).

Thylakoids are flattened **membranous sacs**, and the grana give the chloroplast a large membrane surface for the light reactions.

Key idea: the stroma surrounds them, and the stroma is where the Calvin cycle takes place.
cards.searchQuery: grana stacks of thylakoids chloroplast structure

cards.title: What are the pores on a leaf surface through which $\ce{CO2}$ enters and $\ce{O2}$ exits?
cards.body:
Stomata (singular, stoma).

Each is bordered by two **guard cells** that open and close it. Water vapor also exits through them.

Watch out: closing stomata saves water but cuts off $\ce{CO2}$ supply, which is the root of photorespiration.
cards.searchQuery: stomata leaf pores gas exchange guard cells CO2 O2

cards.title: Which pigment, found in the reaction centers, directly participates in the light reactions by passing excited electrons on?
cards.body:
Chlorophyll $a$.

Other pigments, such as chlorophyll $b$ and carotenoids, pass the energy they absorb to chlorophyll $a$.

Key idea: only chlorophyll $a$ in the **reaction center** converts light energy to chemical energy.
cards.searchQuery: chlorophyll a reaction center pigment light reactions

cards.title: Why do leaves look green?
cards.body:
Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue-violet and red light and reflects or transmits green.

The light we see is what the pigments **don't absorb**.

Tip: autumn colors show up when chlorophyll breaks down and the carotenoids already present become visible.
cards.searchQuery: why leaves are green chlorophyll absorbs red and blue reflects green

cards.title: What is the function of accessory pigments such as chlorophyll $b$ and carotenoids?
cards.body:
They absorb additional wavelengths and pass the energy to chlorophyll $a$.

They broaden the range of light a plant can use. Carotenoids also provide **photoprotection**, absorbing excess light energy that could damage chlorophyll.

Key idea: this energy passes between pigments in light-harvesting complexes.
cards.searchQuery: accessory pigments chlorophyll b carotenoids function photoprotection absorb wavelengths

cards.title: What is the graph of the rate of photosynthesis plotted against the wavelength of light called?
cards.body:
The action spectrum.

It shows which wavelengths are **actually effective**. It resembles the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll but is broader because of accessory pigments.

Example: Engelmann's experiment used bacteria that clustered where algae made the most $\ce{O2}$ under red and blue light.
cards.searchQuery: action spectrum photosynthesis rate vs wavelength Engelmann

cards.title: What are the three products of the light reactions of photosynthesis?
cards.body:
ATP, NADPH and $\ce{O2}$.

ATP and NADPH carry energy and electrons to the **Calvin cycle**, while $\ce{O2}$ is released as a by-product of splitting water.

Key idea: the light reactions convert solar energy into chemical energy.
cards.searchQuery: products of light reactions ATP NADPH oxygen photosynthesis

cards.title: What are the two main parts of a photosystem?
cards.body:
A reaction-center complex and several light-harvesting complexes (antenna).

The antenna pigments absorb photons and pass the energy toward the **reaction center**, where a special pair of chlorophyll $a$ molecules gives up an excited electron to the primary electron acceptor.

Key idea: this electron transfer is the first step in converting light energy into chemical energy.
cards.searchQuery: photosystem structure reaction center light-harvesting complex antenna pigments

cards.title: Which photosystem has a reaction-center chlorophyll $a$ called P700?
cards.body:
Photosystem I.

The name reflects the wavelength of light it absorbs best, **$700\,\mathrm{nm}$**. Photosystem II's reaction center, P680, absorbs best at $680\,\mathrm{nm}$.

Tip: PSI sends electrons on to make NADPH.
cards.searchQuery: photosystem I P700 reaction center chlorophyll NADPH

cards.title: What is the final electron acceptor of the light reactions?
cards.body:
$\ce{NADP+}$

It is reduced to $\ce{NADPH}$ by photosystem I's electrons, via the enzyme NADP$^+$ reductase.

Watch out: $\ce{NADP+}$ in chloroplasts is the counterpart of $\ce{O2}$ in the mitochondrial chain.
cards.searchQuery: final electron acceptor light reactions NADP+ NADPH photosystem I

cards.title: What is the process called by which chloroplasts make ATP using light energy and chemiosmosis?
cards.body:
Photophosphorylation.

Electron flow pumps $\ce{H+}$ into the thylakoid space, and the gradient drives **ATP synthase** in the thylakoid membrane.

Key idea: it is the light-driven analog of oxidative phosphorylation.
cards.searchQuery: photophosphorylation chloroplast ATP synthesis light chemiosmosis

cards.title: How does cyclic electron flow differ from linear electron flow, and why might a plant use it?
cards.body:
In cyclic flow, electrons from photosystem I return to the cytochrome complex. It makes ATP but no NADPH and no $\ce{O2}$.

Photosystem II isn't used, so water isn't split. It lets the chloroplast make **extra ATP** to meet the Calvin cycle's needs.

Why: the Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH in a ratio of $3:2$, while linear flow makes slightly less ATP than that.
cards.searchQuery: cyclic electron flow vs linear photosystem I ATP only no NADPH

cards.title: In chloroplasts, $\ce{H+}$ accumulates in which compartment, forming the gradient that drives ATP synthase?
cards.body:
The thylakoid space (lumen).

$\ce{H+}$ comes from splitting water and from pumping by the electron transport chain. It then flows into the **stroma** through ATP synthase.

Watch out: the ATP is made in the stroma, exactly where the Calvin cycle uses it.
cards.searchQuery: thylakoid space lumen proton gradient ATP synthase stroma

cards.title: Compare chemiosmosis in chloroplasts and mitochondria: where does $\ce{H+}$ build up, and what powers the pumping?
cards.body:
Chloroplasts: $\ce{H+}$ builds up in the thylakoid space, powered by **light**. Mitochondria: it builds up in the intermembrane space, powered by **redox energy from food**.

In both, $\ce{H+}$ flows down its gradient through ATP synthase to make ATP.

Key idea: the ATP synthase in each is oriented so that ATP is made on the side where $\ce{H+}$ exits (the stroma or the matrix).
cards.searchQuery: chemiosmosis chloroplast vs mitochondria comparison thylakoid space intermembrane space

cards.title: What happens at the molecular level when a chlorophyll molecule absorbs a photon?
cards.body:
One of its electrons is boosted to a higher-energy orbital.

The molecule is now in an **excited state**. In a pigment of the antenna it passes the energy on, and in the reaction center it passes the electron to an electron acceptor.

Watch out: an isolated chlorophyll releases the energy as heat or fluorescence, whereas in the thylakoid membrane the electron is captured.
cards.searchQuery: chlorophyll absorbs photon excited electron higher energy state reaction center

cards.title: What is the incorporation of $\ce{CO2}$ from the air into an organic molecule called?
cards.body:
Carbon fixation.

In the Calvin cycle, rubisco **fixes** $\ce{CO2}$ by attaching it to RuBP, producing 3-phosphoglycerate.

Watch out: carbon fixation by itself doesn't need the light's energy, but later steps need ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.
cards.searchQuery: carbon fixation definition CO2 into organic molecule Calvin cycle

cards.title: Name the three phases of the Calvin cycle in order.
cards.body:
Carbon fixation, reduction, and regeneration of the $\ce{CO2}$ acceptor (RuBP).

Fixation attaches $\ce{CO2}$ to RuBP. Reduction uses ATP and NADPH to make **G3P**. Regeneration uses more ATP to rebuild RuBP from G3P.

Key idea: for every three turns, one net G3P leaves the cycle.
cards.searchQuery: Calvin cycle three phases carbon fixation reduction regeneration RuBP

cards.title: What 3-carbon sugar is the direct product that leaves the Calvin cycle and is used to make glucose and other organic molecules?
cards.body:
G3P (glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate).

Two G3P molecules can combine to build **glucose** and other carbohydrates. G3P is also the starting material for many other organic compounds.

Watch out: the Calvin cycle's immediate output is G3P, not glucose.
cards.searchQuery: G3P glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate Calvin cycle output sugar

cards.title: Which 5-carbon sugar bisphosphate accepts $\ce{CO2}$ in the Calvin cycle?
cards.body:
RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate).

Rubisco joins $\ce{CO2}$ to **RuBP**, and the product splits into two 3-phosphoglycerate molecules.

Key idea: RuBP is regenerated at the end of each turn, so the cycle can continue.
cards.searchQuery: RuBP ribulose bisphosphate CO2 acceptor Calvin cycle rubisco

cards.title: Why is it misleading to call the Calvin cycle the "dark reactions"?
cards.body:
It depends on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, and in most plants it runs in the light.

Without the light reactions the supply of **ATP and NADPH** would run out and the cycle would stop.

Key idea: it doesn't directly need light, but it isn't independent of it.
cards.searchQuery: Calvin cycle dark reactions misnomer depends on light reactions ATP NADPH

cards.title: What name is given to plants that fix $\ce{CO2}$ directly with rubisco, forming a 3-carbon compound as the first product?
cards.body:
C3 plants.

The first stable product is 3-phosphoglycerate. Most plants are C3, including rice, wheat and soybeans.

Watch out: in hot, dry conditions, when stomata close, C3 plants lose carbon to **photorespiration**.
cards.searchQuery: C3 plants definition rubisco 3-phosphoglycerate rice wheat soybeans

cards.title: Which enzyme in the mesophyll cells of C4 plants fixes $\ce{CO2}$ into a 4-carbon compound and doesn't bind $\ce{O2}$?
cards.body:
PEP carboxylase.

It adds $\ce{CO2}$ to **PEP** (phosphoenolpyruvate), forming oxaloacetate. Unlike rubisco, it has a high affinity for $\ce{CO2}$ and no oxygenase activity.

Key idea: so it can fix $\ce{CO2}$ even when the stomata are mostly closed.
cards.searchQuery: PEP carboxylase C4 plants mesophyll CO2 fixation oxaloacetate

cards.title: What does CAM stand for in CAM photosynthesis?
cards.body:
Crassulacean acid metabolism.

It is named after the stonecrop family, **Crassulaceae**, in which it was discovered. Plants open their stomata at night, fix $\ce{CO2}$ into organic acids, and use it by day.

Example: cacti, pineapples and many succulents.
cards.searchQuery: CAM photosynthesis crassulacean acid metabolism meaning succulents

cards.title: C4 plants avoid most photorespiration. Why aren't all plants C4?
cards.body:
The C4 pathway costs extra ATP, so it pays off only where photorespiration would be large.

In **hot, sunny climates** the benefit outweighs the cost. In cool, moist climates, C3 plants do as well or better.

Example: corn and sugarcane thrive in warm regions, while wheat and rice are C3.
cards.searchQuery: C4 pathway extra ATP cost benefit hot climates vs C3 plants

cards.title: Why does closing stomata on a hot day raise the fraction of rubisco's reactions with $\ce{O2}$?
cards.body:
It cuts off $\ce{CO2}$ entry while the light reactions keep making $\ce{O2}$.

$\ce{CO2}$ in the leaf drops as it is used up, and $\ce{O2}$ builds up, so rubisco **encounters more $\ce{O2}$ relative to $\ce{CO2}$**.

Key idea: closing stomata saves water but at the cost of photosynthetic efficiency in C3 plants.
cards.searchQuery: stomata closed hot day CO2 drops O2 rises rubisco photorespiration

cards.title: Which molecules does the Calvin cycle return to the light reactions after it uses up ATP and NADPH?
cards.body:
ADP, inorganic phosphate ($\mathrm{P_i}$) and $\ce{NADP+}$.

The light reactions **recharge** them into ATP and NADPH, which supply the Calvin cycle again.

Key idea: the two stages form a closed loop of carriers, linked by light.
cards.searchQuery: Calvin cycle returns ADP NADP+ to light reactions recycling carriers

cards.title: In which chloroplast membrane system are the photosystems and electron transport chain embedded?
cards.body:
The thylakoid membranes.

Their large surface area, with stacking in grana, holds many **photosystems and ATP synthases**.

Key idea: the thylakoid membrane in chloroplasts corresponds to the inner membrane in mitochondria, where the respiratory chain is embedded.
cards.searchQuery: photosystems electron transport chain thylakoid membrane chloroplast location
